question: Can a class-balanced LightGBM model with pairwise co-use features flag dangerous polypharmacy better than a standard MLP surrogate that sees only the raw per-substance levels, on a public substance-use dataset with a rule-based danger label?
method: UCI Drug Consumption (quantified); use = level>=3; polypharmacy = >=5 substances used; dangerous = polypharmacy AND an a-priori sedation-risk co-use pair. One stratified 70/30 split; 3-fold CV on training data for hyperparameters and decision threshold; model seeds 42-44; PR-AUC main metric, F1 and ROC-AUC secondary.
baseline: Standardised MLPClassifier (64-32 hidden units) on the 18 raw substance levels; alpha tuned by CV. Stands in for the neural reward model; not the paper's neural bandit.
improved: Class-balanced LightGBM on raw levels + total substance count + all 153 pairwise co-use indicators; small CV grid over num_leaves and n_estimators.
notes: Stand-in rule-based label, not clinical truth. The improved feature set contains the exact pairwise indicators used to define the label, so the gain partly reflects label construction. Only one train/test split was used (split-once rule), so std covers model seeds 42-44 only, not split variability. Threshold for F1 chosen on training out-of-fold predictions. Test set was not used for any selection. Semer (near-constant, fictitious drug) excluded. Dataset is small (about 1.9k rows), so no subsampling was needed. Substance columns are located by normalised name across features and targets.
